detailed_analysis:
### Overview and Objective

The goal of this study was to locate indium (In), tin (Sn), and lead (Pb) solder deposits within a copper coupon and, where possible, estimate their thicknesses using spectral X-ray transmission imaging. In this technique, a broadband X-ray beam passes through the sample and the transmitted intensity is recorded across ~2000 energy channels at each of the 80x80 spatial positions. Each element leaves a distinctive fingerprint: a sudden drop in transmitted intensity at its characteristic K-absorption edge (In near 27.9 keV, Sn near 29.2 keV, and Pb near 88.0 keV). Locating these edge signatures pixel-by-pixel is the most direct route to a chemical map.

### What the Statistical Decomposition (NMF) Told Us

A blind statistical decomposition of the raw data was performed first to survey the dominant patterns. This approach worked well as an exploratory tool but was fundamentally limited for the chemical mapping task. The reason is physical: transmission data combine attenuation effects multiplicatively (following the Beer-Lambert law), whereas the decomposition assumes signals add together linearly. As a result, the recovered components largely captured the shape of the X-ray source spectrum and detector behavior rather than clean element-specific signatures.

Component 1 was the most reliable in the sense that its model prediction closely tracked the measured data across the full energy range — the reconstruction and the measurement essentially overlaid one another, indicating high fidelity. Physically, however, this component represents the transmitted source continuum through the copper matrix, not a specific solder. Importantly, its abundance map revealed several dark circular blobs — regions of strongly suppressed transmission — which mark the locations of dense, high-attenuation features. Notably, the map shows roughly four such dark blobs, but (as detailed below) only two of these carry a confirmed Pb K-edge; the remaining blobs are best interpreted as other high-attenuation features (e.g., candidate Sn/In-bearing or simply thick copper features) that could not be independently identified from the edge maps and should not be assumed to be lead. The spectral wiggles this component showed near 58–68 keV were traced to the tungsten anode emission lines of the X-ray tube itself (W Ka1/Kb near 59.3/67.2 keV, consistent with the plot and confirmed by the provided source-only baseline), not to sample chemistry.

Components 2 through 5 were each dominated by an intense spike confined to the very lowest energy channels (below the 5 keV validity threshold), a classic signature of detector artifacts and low-energy noise rather than genuine material edges. For Component 2 in particular, the NMF basis shows a spike near ~95,000 intensity while the corresponding measured spectrum peaks near ~28,000 — a greater than threefold amplitude mismatch — further indicating this component is not a physically meaningful material signature. Although their reconstructions matched the measured spectra reasonably well numerically, the spectral information these components carried was not chemically diagnostic. Their abundance maps are likewise limited in value: the Component 2 high-purity region comprises only 1.3% of pixels (86 pixels), and the Components 3–5 abundance maps display classic scattered, speckled high-purity contours (many small, disconnected red rings) characteristic of salt-and-pepper noise rather than structured deposits. Accordingly, these components should not be used to infer the presence or composition of specific deposits, and no elemental assignment is drawn from them. In short, the decomposition was useful for confirming that the raw-transmission unmixing is dominated by source-continuum and detector effects, motivating a physics-based approach, but it could not on its own identify which element any deposit contained.

### Physics-Based Edge Mapping: The Decisive Evidence

To directly answer the elemental question, a targeted physics-based analysis was applied. The raw spectra were first converted to optical density (absorbance) using the supplied source-only baseline, which linearizes the attenuation problem and makes absorption edges far easier to detect. The height of the step at each element's K-edge was then measured at every pixel. Because the In and Sn edges lie only ~1.3 keV apart, a joint two-edge fit was used to separate them, while the well-isolated Pb edge near 88 keV was measured directly.

The **Pb map is the standout, high-confidence result.** The lead edge-step and derived thickness maps both show two clear, spatially compact, roughly circular deposits — one in the upper-left and one in the lower-central region of the field — standing well above a quiet background. These locations coincide precisely with two of the dark, high-attenuation blobs seen in the Component 1 abundance map, providing independent cross-validation between the two analysis methods. The value distribution shows a well-populated tail rising above the near-zero background (extending to ~0.8–1.0 Delta-OD), consistent with genuine, localized lead-bearing material of measurable areal density.

The **Sn result is at or below the detection limit.** The tin edge-step, thickness, and signal-quality maps all show a sparse, speckled 'salt-and-pepper' pattern rather than solid, well-defined deposits: the Sn_Thickness histogram has mean/std of 0.00/0.00, the Sn_Edge_Step histogram is spiked at zero (mean 0.02, std 0.08, with roughly 5900 of 6400 pixels in the zero bin), and the spatial maps show no coherent structure. This is textbook salt-and-pepper noise with no spatial organization. Accordingly, tin is best reported as not detected above the noise floor / at or below the detection limit of this measurement, rather than as a localized presence. The scattered nature of the Sn maps mirrors the speckle in Components 3–5, but because both distributions are noise-like this shared appearance does not constitute independent corroboration and no such cross-claim is made.

The **In distribution could not be recovered.** Because the indium K-edge sits immediately below the much stronger tin edge, the two could not be cleanly separated at the available energy resolution and signal levels, and the indium map did not survive quality control. Its absence should therefore be read as a limitation of the measurement/analysis, not as proof that indium is absent from the coupon.

### Unified Physical Model

Taking all scales of analysis together, a consistent picture emerges. The copper coupon acts as a uniform attenuating matrix (captured cleanly by the well-reconstructed background component) into which discrete high-attenuation features are embedded as compact, roughly circular regions. At least two of these features are confidently identified as lead-rich, based on their unmistakable 88 keV edge signatures and their agreement with the independently derived high-attenuation blobs in the Component 1 map. The remaining dark blobs in the Component 1 map do not carry a confirmed Pb edge and cannot be assigned a composition from the present data. Tin is at or below the detection limit and is not confidently mapped, and indium remains unresolved due to its spectral overlap with tin. The thickness (areal density) estimates should be treated as approximate — useful for confirming the presence and relative density of the lead deposits, and not meaningful for tin.

### Recommendations

Confident elemental localization is achievable for lead with the current data. To recover indium and firm up tin, improvements in energy resolution or counting statistics around the closely spaced 27.9/29.2 keV edges would be required, along with continued use of absorbance (source-normalized) processing rather than raw-intensity decomposition for any quantitative claims. Characterizing the remaining (non-Pb) high-attenuation blobs would also benefit from complementary measurements.

### Key Evidence
- **[Global_Analysis] Component 1 Analysis**: The measured spectrum and model reconstruction overlay almost perfectly, confirming this component reliably represents the transmitted source continuum through the copper matrix; its abundance map reveals roughly four dark circular high-attenuation blobs, of which only two are subsequently confirmed as lead-bearing by the Pb edge maps.
- **[Global_Analysis] Component 2 Analysis**: Spectrally dominated by a low-energy detector artifact (basis spike ~95,000 vs. measured peak ~28,000, confined below the 5 keV validity threshold); with a high-purity region of only 1.3% of pixels and non-diagnostic spectral content, it does not support an elemental or 'dense deposit' assignment.
- **[Global_Analysis] Custom Analysis: Pb_Edge_Step**: Shows two clear, spatially compact circular lead deposits (upper-left and lower-central) standing well above background, with a histogram tail extending to ~0.8–1.0 Delta-OD — the highest-confidence elemental localization in the study.
- **[Global_Analysis] Custom Analysis: Pb_Thickness**: Reproduces the same two circular lead deposits in areal-density units, cross-validating the edge-step map and providing an approximate thickness estimate.
- **[Global_Analysis] Custom Analysis: Sn_Edge_Step**: Displays a salt-and-pepper distribution spiked at zero (mean 0.02, std 0.08; ~5900 of 6400 pixels in the zero bin) with no coherent spatial structure, indicating tin is at or below the detection limit.
- **[Global_Analysis] Custom Analysis: Sn_Thickness**: Histogram mean/std of 0.00/0.00 confirms no quantifiable tin areal density above the noise floor.
- **[Global_Analysis] Custom Analysis: Sn_SNR**: Confirms that the tin edge signal is weak and scattered across most pixels, reinforcing that tin is not detected above the noise floor.
- **[Global_Analysis] NMF Summary Grid**: Provides the side-by-side comparison showing that four of five statistical components are dominated by low-energy artifacts, motivating the shift to physics-based edge mapping for elemental identification.

scientific_claims.claim: In spectral X-ray transmission imaging of a multi-metal solder coupon, lead deposits can be confidently localized and their areal density estimated using the isolated high-energy K-absorption edge, whereas indium and tin cannot be reliably separated because their K-edges lie only about one keV apart.
scientific_claims.scientific_impact: Establishing which elements are separable at a given energy resolution defines the practical limits of energy-resolving photon-counting detectors for non-destructive elemental mapping and quality control of electronic solders and interconnects.
scientific_claims.has_anyone_question: Has anyone shown that closely spaced K-absorption edges of neighboring elements cannot be reliably separated in spectral X-ray transmission imaging when the energy resolution approaches the edge spacing?

scientific_claims.claim: Linear statistical decomposition of raw X-ray transmission spectra tends to capture source-continuum and detector artifacts rather than element-specific absorption edges, so converting to absorbance before analysis is strongly preferable for recovering physically meaningful elemental maps.
scientific_claims.scientific_impact: Demonstrating that Beer-Lambert nonlinearity undermines additive unmixing of raw transmission data would guide preprocessing standards and prevent misinterpretation of blind decomposition components as physical chemical phases.
scientific_claims.has_anyone_question: Has anyone demonstrated that converting X-ray transmission data to absorbance before statistical unmixing improves recovery of element-specific absorption edges relative to source and detector artifacts?

Amplitudes a_In,a_Sn are the edge-step heights, gated by residual SNR>3 and I0 flux>20. Pb K-edge (88 keV, isolated) uses measure_edge_step directly. Thickness = edge_step / delta(mu/rho) with mu from NIST tables at edge +/-0.5 keV (areal density).. [Data Source: Raw Data (Medium quality, SNR≈29.3)]

dynamic_analysis_records.target: Compute per-pixel transmittance by dividing the sample cube by the provided I0 flat-field baseline cube on the same grid, then take -ln(I/I0) to obtain optical density (absorbance) vs energy, restricting to energies above 5 keV. For each of the three target elements (In, Pb, Sn), use the measure_edge_step helper to quantify the K-edge absorption jump at each pixel: In K-edge near 27.9 keV, Sn K-edge near 29.2 keV, and Pb K-edge near 88.0 keV. Because the In and Sn K-edges are only ~1.3 keV apart (near the 0.2 keV energy resolution / 0.1 keV bin width), measure their edge steps in their respective narrow windows and treat overlapping-signal pixels as mixed. Produce a spatial edge-step-height map for each element indicating where that element is present, plus a measurable/flux gate so weak-signal pixels are masked. Then convert each element's edge-step height to material thickness using the attenuation helper to obtain mu(E) across the K-edge for that element (derived from the element name), giving thickness = edge_step / (delta_mu). Report both presence (edge-step) maps and thickness maps for In, Pb, and Sn.
dynamic_analysis_records.script:
def analyze_feature(data, axis, reconstruction=None, auxiliary=None):
    from scilink.skills._shared.edge_step import measure_edge_step
    from scilink.skills._shared.xray_attenuation import attenuation
    import scipy.optimize

    H, W, E = data.shape
    N = H * W
    energy = np.asarray(axis, dtype=float)

    # ---- I0 baseline ----
    if auxiliary and "I0 flat-field baseline cube (no sample) on the same grid" in auxiliary:
        i0 = np.asarray(auxiliary["I0 flat-field baseline cube (no sample) on the same grid"], dtype=float)
    else:
        i0 = np.full_like(data, np.nanmedian(data), dtype=float)

    raw = np.asarray(data, dtype=float)
    # denoised for shape-based OD if available
    src = raw
    if reconstruction is not None:
        rec = np.asarray(reconstruction, dtype=float)
        if rec.shape == raw.shape:
            src = rec

    # ---- Optical density (absorbance) ----
    eps = 1.0
    T = np.clip(src, 1e-3, None) / np.clip(i0, eps, None)
    T = np.clip(T, 1e-4, None)
    OD = -np.log(T)  # (H,W,E)

    # restrict to > 5 keV validity via mask on energy
    e_valid = energy > 5.0

    # =====================================================================
    # PART A: Pb K-edge at 88 keV -- isolated, use helper directly on RAW
    # =====================================================================
    pb_edge = 88.0
    pb_res = measure_edge_step(raw, i0, energy, pb_edge,
                               pre_gap=2.0, post_gap=1.0, win_width=4.0,
                               low_e_cut_kev=5.0, flux_floor_counts=20.0,
                               auto_center=True, search_tol_kev=2.0)
    Pb_step = np.asarray(pb_res['edge_step'], dtype=float)
    Pb_snr = np.asarray(pb_res.get('snr', np.zeros_like(Pb_step)), dtype=float)
    Pb_gate = Pb_snr > 3.0
    Pb_step_map = np.where(Pb_gate, Pb_step, 0.0)
    Pb_step_map = np.clip(Pb_step_map, 0.0, None)

    # =====================================================================
    # PART B: JOINT TWO-EDGE FIT for In (27.94) and Sn (29.20) in 26-31 keV
    #   Model over narrow window w:
    #     OD(E) = c0 + c1*(E-Ec)
    #             + a_In * H(E - E_In)
    #             + a_Sn * H(E - E_Sn)
    #   where H is a smoothed step (erf) with fixed edge width sigma.
    #   a_In, a_Sn >= 0 are the edge-step heights. Linear least squares
    #   with fixed step shapes -> per-pixel NNLS. This resolves two
    #   closely-spaced edges that a single differential window cannot.
    # =====================================================================
    E_In = 27.94
    E_Sn = 29.20
    win_lo, win_hi = 26.0, 31.0
    wmask = (energy >= win_lo) & (energy <= win_hi) & e_valid
    Ew = energy[wmask]
    ODw = OD.reshape(N, E)[:, wmask]  # (N, k)

    from scipy.special import erf
    sigma = 0.15  # keV edge smoothing (~resolution/binning)
    Ec = 0.5 * (win_lo + win_hi)

    def step(Evec, E0):
        return 0.5 * (1.0 + erf((Evec - E0) / (np.sqrt(2.0) * sigma)))

    # Design matrix columns: [1, (E-Ec), step_In, step_Sn]
    col_const = np.ones_like(Ew)
    col_lin = (Ew - Ec)
    col_In = step(Ew, E_In)
    col_Sn = step(Ew, E_Sn)
    Aall = np.column_stack([col_const, col_lin, col_In, col_Sn])  # (k,4)

    # For per-pixel positivity on the two step amplitudes only, we split:
    # first remove the linear continuum via ordinary LSQ but constrain
    # step amps >=0. Use bounded lstsq per pixel is slow (6400 px). Instead:
    # Solve unconstrained LSQ vectorized, then clamp step amps to >=0 and
    # refit continuum. This is stable and fast.
    # Unconstrained pseudo-inverse:
    pinv = np.linalg.pinv(Aall)  # (4,k)
    coef = ODw @ pinv.T          # (N,4)
    a_In = coef[:, 2]
    a_Sn = coef[:, 3]

    # Refine: clamp negatives, and reduce In/Sn cross-talk by a single
    # joint NNLS on the two step columns after removing fitted continuum
    # for pixels flagged as candidate (speeds up + improves separation).
    cont = coef[:, 0:1] * col_const[None, :] + coef[:, 1:2] * col_lin[None, :]
    resid = ODw - cont  # (N,k) continuum-removed OD

    # Two-column design for NNLS
    B = np.column_stack([col_In, col_Sn])  # (k,2)
    # Normal equations for 2x2 NNLS solved analytically w/ nonneg clamp:
    BtB = B.T @ B                # (2,2)
    Btr = resid @ B              # (N,2)
    # Solve BtB x = Btr for all pixels
    try:
        invBtB = np.linalg.inv(BtB)
        xsol = Btr @ invBtB.T    # (N,2)
    except np.linalg.LinAlgError:
        xsol = np.column_stack([a_In, a_Sn])

    a_In = xsol[:, 0]
    a_Sn = xsol[:, 1]

    # Nonnegativity: if either negative, redo constrained (drop neg col)
    neg_In = a_In < 0
    neg_Sn = a_Sn < 0
    # If In negative -> set 0, refit Sn alone
    if np.any(neg_In):
        sn_only = (resid[neg_In] @ col_Sn) / (col_Sn @ col_Sn)
        a_In[neg_In] = 0.0
        a_Sn[neg_In] = sn_only
    if np.any(neg_Sn):
        in_only = (resid[neg_Sn] @ col_In) / (col_In @ col_In)
        a_Sn[neg_Sn] = 0.0
        a_In[neg_Sn] = in_only
    a_In = np.clip(a_In, 0.0, None)
    a_Sn = np.clip(a_Sn, 0.0, None)

    # ---- Flux / measurable gate for In & Sn ----
    # Median post-edge I0 flux around 30 keV must exceed floor
    post_e = (energy >= 29.5) & (energy <= 31.5)
    flux_post = np.median(i0.reshape(N, E)[:, post_e], axis=1)
    flux_gate = flux_post > 20.0

    # Residual-based SNR: signal amplitude vs fit residual RMS
    model = cont + a_In[:, None] * col_In[None, :] + a_Sn[:, None] * col_Sn[None, :]
    rms = np.sqrt(np.mean((ODw - model) ** 2, axis=1)) + 1e-6
    snr_In = a_In / rms
    snr_Sn = a_Sn / rms

    In_gate = (snr_In > 3.0) & flux_gate
    Sn_gate = (snr_Sn > 3.0) & flux_gate

    In_step_map = np.where(In_gate, a_In, 0.0).reshape(H, W)
    Sn_step_map = np.where(Sn_gate, a_Sn, 0.0).reshape(H, W)

    # =====================================================================
    # PART C: Thickness = edge_step / delta_mu   (delta_mu across edge)
    # =====================================================================
    def delta_mu(elem, edge_kev):
        e_lo = np.array([edge_kev - 0.5])
        e_hi = np.array([edge_kev + 0.5])
        mu_lo = attenuation(elem, e_lo)[0]
        mu_hi = attenuation(elem, e_hi)[0]
        return abs(mu_hi - mu_lo)

    dmu_In = delta_mu('In', E_In)
    dmu_Sn = delta_mu('Sn', E_Sn)
    dmu_Pb = delta_mu('Pb', pb_edge)

    def safe_div(step_map, dmu):
        if dmu is None or not np.isfinite(dmu) or dmu <= 0:
            return np.zeros_like(step_map)
        return step_map / dmu

    # thickness in cm (mu/rho in cm^2/g * rho). Since attenuation returns
    # mass mu without density, thickness = step/(delta(mu/rho)) has units
    # of areal density (g/cm^2). Report as areal density proxy (a.u./thickness).
    In_thick = safe_div(In_step_map, dmu_In)
    Sn_thick = safe_div(Sn_step_map, dmu_Sn)
    Pb_thick = safe_div(Pb_step_map, dmu_Pb)

    # clean NaNs
    for arr in (In_step_map, Sn_step_map, Pb_step_map, In_thick, Sn_thick, Pb_thick):
        np.nan_to_num(arr, copy=False, nan=0.0, posinf=0.0, neginf=0.0)

    maps = {
        "In_Edge_Step": In_step_map,
        "Sn_Edge_Step": Sn_step_map,
        "Pb_Edge_Step": Pb_step_map,
        "In_Thickness": In_thick,
        "Sn_Thickness": Sn_thick,
        "Pb_Thickness": Pb_thick,
        "In_SNR": snr_In.reshape(H, W),
        "Sn_SNR": snr_Sn.reshape(H, W),
    }
    units = {
        "In_Edge_Step": "Delta-OD",
        "Sn_Edge_Step": "Delta-OD",
        "Pb_Edge_Step": "Delta-OD",
        "In_Thickness": "g/cm^2 (areal density)",
        "Sn_Thickness": "g/cm^2 (areal density)",
        "Pb_Thickness": "g/cm^2 (areal density)",
        "In_SNR": "a.u.",
        "Sn_SNR": "a.u.",
    }
    desc = ("Per-pixel OD = -ln(I/I0). In(27.94) and Sn(29.20) K-edges, only 1.26 keV "
            "apart, are resolved by a JOINT two-edge fit over 26-31 keV: linear continuum "
            "plus two fixed-width (sigma=0.15 keV) erf step functions at the two edge energies, "
            "solved per pixel with nonnegativity so the Sn pre-window no longer straddles the In "
            "edge (kills the cross-talk that filled 96% of the field). Amplitudes a_In,a_Sn are the "
            "edge-step heights, gated by residual SNR>3 and I0 flux>20. Pb K-edge (88 keV, isolated) "

issues.problem: The In edge-step map is spatially incoherent salt-and-pepper noise, not a coherent solder region. Solders are localized deposits — the In map should show contiguous patches, but instead ~43.5% of pixels are randomly scattered across the ENTIRE field with no morphological structure, which is the signature of noise passing the SNR gate rather than a real localized In signal. The root cause is the pseudo-I0 fallback: no flat-field baseline was supplied, so I0 was estimated as the 95th-percentile spectrum across all pixels. Near the In/Sn K-edges (27.9/29.2 keV) the mean spectrum shows only weak, broad bumps sitting on a low continuum (~50-100 counts) — this is a flux-starved, low-contrast region where a percentile-based pseudo-I0 creates spurious per-pixel OD steps. Corrective direction: (1) require and use a true I0 flat-field baseline instead of the percentile fallback (this is the dominant fabrication source); (2) verify the actual In K-edge location against the data — the metadata In K-edge is ~27.9 keV but tabulated In K-edge is 27.94 keV while Sn is 29.20 keV, and with 0.2 keV resolution the 0.8 keV windows are marginal; and (3) demand spatial coherence (connected-component / contiguity check) rather than a per-pixel SNR>3 gate, which admits isolated noise pixels.
